title: "Here, read my book"
hookLine: the one given his record in his right hand says to everyone: here, read my book (69:19)

cards: A kid with a good report card doesn't fold it into a backpack. It comes out at the kitchen table: look, read this. The other kind stays folded, and the kid hopes nobody asks.
Same paper, opposite instinct. Surah al-Haqqah takes that urge, to show or to hide, and sets it on the Day of Judgment. One person is handed a book and turns to everyone around them: here, read it.

teach.b: Verse nineteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book!" The Arabic begins with haa'umu, a call that means here, take it, come and look.
The record, kitab, is the book of a person's deeds; elsewhere the Qur'an speaks of noble scribes, angels who write down what people do.

teach.h: THE RECORD IN THE RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: In the Qur'an's picture, the right hand is the sign of a good outcome.

teach.h: I WAS SURE I'D MEET MY RECKONING.
teach.b: And the person's next words, in verse twenty, are a confession of how they lived: I was sure I would meet my reckoning. They didn't get there by never thinking about the day, but by thinking about it all along.
The verses go on to a high garden with fruit hanging low, and the words: eat and drink, in return for what you sent ahead in days gone by. Then the surah turns.

teach.h: THE LEFT HAND: I WISH I'D NEVER.
teach.b: The one given the book in his left hand says the opposite: oh, I wish I'd never been given my book, never known my account. My wealth didn't help me. My power is gone from me.
Same book, opposite instinct. One holds it out; one wishes it didn't exist. Muslims believe this scene is real, and it's meant to shape ordinary days now.
The question it plants is simple. If today were written down in a book you'd be handed later, which parts would you hold out to the room?

how: Muslims believe each person's deeds are recorded and that on the Day of Judgment the record is given in the right hand or the left; some recall this when examining their day, and pray to be given their book in the right hand.

o: a place in the garden where the righteous rest
the call to prayer, saying come to the prayer
here, take it: what the joyful one says of the record

I wish I'd never been given it

they say: I was sure I would meet my reckoning.
in the Qur'an's picture, the right hand means a good outcome
the one given the record in the right hand rejoices.

he says his wealth didn't help and his power is gone.

games.q: you're handed your book in your right hand. what do you do, by 69:19?
o: hide it until you read it alone.
hold it out: here, read my book!
games.why: he turns to everyone: here, read my book! the joy of nothing to hide.

practice: Walk back through yesterday like pages in a book, without judging every line. Notice which pages you'd hold out, a kindness, a job done well, a hard thing done honestly, and which you'd turn face down.
Then look ahead to today and choose one thing you'd be glad to have written.

wordCard.voice: Here. The first word of the joyful one in 69:19, given the record in the right hand: here, read my book. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 69:19: here, take, read my book! haa'umu is a call to come and look.

carryVoice: Your line: same book, opposite instinct. A whole week, from the birds to the book. See you tomorrow.
